passage:
Monday. Wasim showed the group his phone: the money he'd put on a friend's hot tip had doubled in three weeks. Everyone cheered. Suraj clapped a beat late. That night he kept thinking he'd been saving carefully for two years and had gone nowhere. He opened a message to his cousin to ask about a loan, then left it unsent.

Friday. Suraj read a long thread about people who lost money on tips, most of whom never posted. He asked Wasim over chai, "Did you ever take a tip that failed?" Wasim rubbed his neck. "Yes. Twice. I don't talk about those."

The following Thursday. Suraj finished a free beginner's guide that explained index funds, spreading money across many things, and how time helps. He deleted the unsent message to his cousin and set a small monthly amount aside instead.

qa.q: How long did it take for Wasim's money to double?
qa.a: Wasim's money had doubled in three weeks.

qa.q: What was Suraj feeling on Monday night, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Suraj felt envious and left behind, since he clapped a beat late and kept thinking he had saved carefully for two years and gone nowhere.

qa.q: What went right in Suraj's choices between Monday and Thursday?
qa.a: He did not borrow, he learned that losers rarely post, and he read about index funds, spreading money out and time before setting aside a small amount.

qa.q: Why might Wasim not mention his failed tips to the group?
qa.a: Wasim rubs his neck and says he doesn't talk about those, which suggests the losses feel embarrassing and the wins are the part that gets shared.

grounding: Suraj envies Wasim's doubled money, nearly borrows to chase it, then learns that survivor stories hide the losers and studies the basics.

passage: Chinmay, you've been gloomy since your friend showed you his profit. Let your Kavitha-aunty tell you about 1992. My friend Revathi put her savings into one company's shares on a tip from her uncle, and in three months she had doubled them. She bought a new sewing machine and silk saris. I felt left behind, like a fool with my money sitting still. So I borrowed from my elder brother, saying it was for a course, and bought the same shares. A month later the whole market crashed. I lost everything I'd borrowed, and it took me two years to repay my brother. The worst part: Revathi had sold just in time, by luck. Nobody talks about the ones who bought late. After that I sat with a proper adviser at the bank and learnt the slow basics: spreading things out, giving them time. So, Chinmay, be happy for your friend. Then go learn the boring way.

qa.q: What did Revathi buy after doubling her savings?
qa.a: Revathi bought a new sewing machine and silk saris.

qa.q: How did young Kavitha feel after Revathi's win?
qa.a: Kavitha felt envious and left behind, like a fool with money sitting still.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Kavitha handled money?
qa.a: Losing the borrowed money and taking two years to repay, then learning the slow basics from a proper adviser at the bank.

qa.q: What does Revathi's lucky exit hide from people like Kavitha?
qa.a: It hides the people who bought late and lost, so her win looked easier and safer than it was.

grounding: An aunt recalls envying a friend's quick win, chasing it with borrowed money and losing, and then learning the slow basics from a qualified adviser.

passage: Divyansh showed Akash the screenshot in the college canteen in Nagpur: a small-company share bought on a tip from a video channel, now worth almost twice as much after six weeks. 'Easy money, bro.' Akash smiled, but all through the afternoon lecture he felt a sour, left-behind ache. He had nothing to invest; his fees were due on Friday. By evening he had a loan app open, the application half filled, the same share's name typed into his notes. Then his phone buzzed: his elder sister asking whether the fee was sorted. He froze. He was about to borrow in his fee week to chase someone else's lucky tip. He closed the app. That night he looked up who had bought that tip late. The comments under the video were full of losses nobody had screenshotted. On Saturday, fees paid, he signed up for the free investor-education sessions run by his college's commerce department.

qa.a: Akash's fees were due on Friday.

qa.q: What was Akash feeling during the afternoon lecture?
qa.a: Akash felt envious and left behind, a sour ache after seeing Divyansh's win.

qa.q: What stopped Akash, and what did he choose instead?
qa.a: His sister's message made him see he was borrowing in his fee week to chase a tip; he closed the app and joined free investor-education sessions.

qa.q: What might Divyansh's screenshot leave out?
qa.a: It leaves out the people who bought the same tip late and lost, whose losses nobody screenshotted.

grounding: Shows envy of a friend's hot-tip win almost leading to borrowing to chase it, and the choice to learn the basics instead.
